phase1.intro:
Every collection this unit has used so far has had a type in angle brackets — ArrayList<String>, HashMap<String, Integer>. That's not decoration.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What is a generic class, conceptually?
dialogue: Back in Unit 1's workshop metaphor: a blueprint describes a shape any house of that design can follow. [[key:A generic class is a blueprint with a placeholder — Box<T> is a blueprint for a box holding some type T]], and T only gets pinned down when you actually build one: Box<String>, Box<Integer>, Box<Student>.

stickyNote.flavor: 🧩 a blueprint with a placeholder type
stickyNote.definition: A generic class like Box<T> has a placeholder type T, pinned down only when you actually instantiate it (Box<String>, Box<Integer>).

dialogue: [[warn:Without generics, a raw ArrayList will happily let you add a String and an Integer to the same list]] — no error until you try to cast one back out and get a ClassCastException, possibly nowhere near where it got added. With ArrayList<String>, the compiler simply refuses to let anything else in.

stickyNote.flavor: 🛡️ the compiler catches it, not a runtime crash
stickyNote.definition: Generics let the compiler reject mismatched types at compile time (ArrayList<String>), instead of letting a raw ArrayList mix types and crash later.

topics.buttonText: What do List<?> and List<? extends Number> mean?
dialogue: [[term:Wildcards]] show up when you don't need to pin the type down exactly — `List<?>` means "a list of something, I don't need to know what," and bounded wildcards like `List<? extends Number>` mean "a list of some type that's at least a Number."

stickyNote.flavor: ❓ some type, or some type at least this general
stickyNote.definition: List<?> means an unknown element type. List<? extends Number> means an unknown type that's at least a Number — enough to read numeric values.

phase1.openingDialogue: Generics turn a class into a reusable blueprint with a placeholder type — catching type mistakes at compile time instead of at runtime. 🧩

phase2.errorMessage:
Test.java:5: error: unexpected type
        ArrayList<int> list = new ArrayList<>();  // ERROR!
                   ^
  required: reference type
  found:    int
1 error
phase2.explanation:
This one's a compile error, not a runtime crash — [[key:generics can't take primitive types]], only reference types.

ArrayList<int> fails because int is a primitive — a raw value, not an object. Generics work by erasure: under the hood the compiler needs every T to be something that can be treated as an Object, and a primitive int simply isn't one. [[warn:the fix isn't obscure, it's just remembering to use the wrapper class]]:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();  // Integer, not int

This is exactly why autoboxing exists: list.add(5) still works, because Java automatically boxes the primitive 5 into an Integer object before it goes in, and unboxes it back to an int when you pull it out with get(). You write ordinary-looking int code; the wrapper conversion happens for you underneath it.

mcq.question:
A method needs to accept a List of any kind of Number (Integer, Double, Long...) and sum the values, but should never be allowed to add new elements to that list. Which parameter type fits best?

A) List<Number> list
B) List<?> list
C) List<? extends Number> list
D) ArrayList<Integer> list

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a generic class Container<T> with:
• Private field: item (T type)
• Constructor that takes T
• Getter: get()
• Setter: set(T item)
• Method: isSame(Container<T> other) — returns true if items are equal

In main:
1. Create Container<String> with "Hello"
2. Create Container<Integer> with 42
3. Create Container<String> with "Hello"
4. Check if the two String containers are the same using isSame()
5. Print all items

phase5.trivia: Java's generics are implemented via type erasure — at compile time ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Integer> are checked as different types, but by the time the class file exists, both have been erased down to plain ArrayList. That's a deliberate backward-compatibility choice: it let generics (added in Java 5, 2004) work with bytecode written years before generics existed.
